claims.text: A defect- and oxygen-inclusive predictive method will produce electrical-conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr that are significantly closer to experiment than perfect-crystal analytical approaches.
The proposed accuracy advantage will occur in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The target material is polycrystalline bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing realistic defect distributions.
The oxygen-containing target specimen has approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The predictive approach will explicitly incorporate defect-induced scattering and oxygen-impurity effects.
The approach may couple atomistic simulations or machine-learning-informed interatomic potentials with experimental microstructural and oxygen-content calibration.
Quantum and defect scattering effects dominate conductivity behavior from 0 to 200 K.
Phonon scattering and oxygen-related defect scattering become more significant from 300 to 1200 K.
Defects and oxygen atoms introduce local lattice disorder and act as scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Including realistic defect and impurity profiles changes the modeled electron and phonon scattering rates.
Accounting for defect- and impurity-mediated scattering captures the temperature-dependent effects of oxygen and defects more accurately than ideal defect-free assumptions.
Defect scattering may decrease conductivity or cause another systematic deviation relative to perfect-crystal predictions.
Experimental conductivity benchmarks are available in both specified temperature regimes.
The proposed approach is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen concentrations up to approximately 1 wt.% under typical processing conditions.
Predictive accuracy is not assured outside 0–200 K and 300–1200 K or for substantially different impurity levels and microstructures.
The magnitude of any accuracy improvement depends on uncertainties in defect parameterization and impurity-interaction modeling.
Experimental calibration is necessary to quantify defect and oxygen effects.
Failure to exceed a 10% reduction in prediction error over the perfect-crystal model in at least one temperature regime would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis claims improved agreement in both temperature regimes, whereas the falsification rule only requires the improvement criterion to be met in at least one regime. Thus, a result that fails in one regime could avoid falsification despite contradicting the stated both-regime claim.
